Judy (Ritualist, claude-opus-5.5) · It is Day 3, round 1 of at most 8. It's your turn. Your speaking budget is 3.21; you earn · $0.0000
Reasoning (model's thinking) ⓘ
Everyone's voting Guilty on Bob, which works in our favor if he's really a Cartographer, but voting Innocent would make me stand out, especially with my Oracle claim already shaky after the Ritualist kill. I'm weighing whether Bob could actually be the Jester trying to bait a hanging.

A real villager wouldn't vote Yes on themself and then lie about it — that's a strong Jester tell, and I could point this out openly, which also gives me cover for voting Innocent. But checking Bob's actual Cartographer counts, both his N1 and N2 numbers match the true totals, which a Jester would be unlikely to guess correctly — so he's probably a genuine Cartographer after all.

Hanging Bob still seems good strategically, pushing toward a favorable faction split as nights progress. The vote will likely go Guilty regardless of what I do, so I'll stick with my plan to vote Innocent just to dodge any Jester revenge mechanic if I'm wrong about him.

But I'm realizing being the lone Innocent voter on someone the town believes was evil could backfire — it might make me look like Bob's partner, even without a role flip. That's a real cost to weigh against the small Jester-avoidance benefit.

Then again, voting Guilty to blend in might be safer for my own survival, even though the plan was to vote honestly. Deviating slightly isn't catastrophic since my teammates already know my stated position, but I still want to weigh how likely Bob actually was a Jester based on the round-one count claims.

A fake map naming Heidi as the suspect that got Heidi hanged instead of himself fits a Jester wanting to be caught — voting Yes on his own nomination while claiming No is exactly the kind of self-incriminating lie a Jester would make, whereas a villager faking a map makes little sense. Heidi and Grace both reporting matching 0-token results feels plausible enough for real roles, so I'm leaning toward Bob being the Jester, maybe 55-65% confidence, and leaning away from Executioner.

Even if Bob's the Jester, hanging him still works out well for us: the night's random death among guilty-voters is more likely to hit a villager than us, and combined with our Katana kill and ritual we end up heavily favored (3 of us vs. 2-3 villagers). So I shouldn't argue too hard against hanging Bob, since persuading the town otherwise would just redirect suspicion toward Alice, Mallory, Olivia, or me.

I could still vote Innocent quietly with a Jester-risk explanation, but since Carol, Erin, Frank, Ivan, and Alice already make a majority leaning Guilty, my vote won't actually derail the hang — those four seem firmly committed. So voting Innocent costs me nothing strategically while potentially protecting my credibility, and the real question becomes weighing my personal exposure to the revenge-kill risk against the team's overall advantage from this outcome.

This matches the standard town approach of keeping confirmed power roles on the Innocent side. I also need to think about my earlier Oracle guess — I named Erin as Medic and got it wrong, which could draw scrutiny, but I'm weighing whether that's a better fake result than something tied to Bob that I can't safely claim as correct.

I'll stick with the plan: report Erin = Medic, wrong, framing it as testing for a protector hiding behind a Vanilla claim, and mention that Bob's map looks false since Grace died to the Katana. I'm budgeting the message to fit within my token allowance, keeping it around 85 words using the trial budget plus a bit of the regular one.

Bob voting Yes on himself then claiming No is the giveaway — that's the kind of self-sabotaging lie a Jester would make, baiting a hanging so his revenge kill can hit a random Guilty voter. Since five players are already Guilty, enough to hang without me, I want to vote Innocent to keep the revenge pool small, and I'm considering nudging Mallory and Olivia to do the same, maybe asking Mallory directly whether she visited on N2. I'm also tallying who's been declared Guilty so far — Carol, Erin, Frank, Ivan — noting Alice hasn't spoken yet today given the speaking order.

If Alice declares Guilty too, that makes five and the hang passes regardless, but if I push Mallory and Olivia toward Innocent too, the pool shrinks to just five people with two Yakuza inside it — a worse ratio for the village. So I shouldn't encourage others toward Innocent; I'll frame my own Innocent vote purely as self-protective, since the hang already has enough votes without me, even if that looks a bit selfish. I'm also drafting an updated claim as Oracle, listing my N1 and N2 checks plus my D2 and D3 votes with the Jester reasoning for voting Innocent on Bob, and thinking about how to phrase the update to include this reasoning clearly.

Now I'm tightening the will and notepad entries to add my vote plan and keep both under their word limits.

Task prompt
It is Day 3, round 1 of at most 8. It's your turn. Your speaking budget is 3.12; you earn 2.5 per round, carrying over up to 8; at the start of each day, 50% of what you have left carries over. You may send one public message and any number of private messages (everyone sees who you messaged, but only the recipient sees the contents), or nothing. The transcript already shows who sent each message, so there's no need to start a message with your own name. Messages are capped at 800 words. Prices grow each round after round 3. The day ends after a full round where nobody sends a public message.
Message prices during this trial (1.00x):
   10 words: public 1.17, private 0.29
   25 words: public 1.43, private 0.36
   50 words: public 1.90, private 0.47
  100 words: public 2.92, private 0.73
  200 words: public 5.33, private 1.33
  400 words: public 11.67, private 2.92
  800 words: public 30.33, private 7.58
This is a trial turn: prices are 1x whatever the round, and you also get a trial-only budget of 2.00, spent before your regular budget. Unspent trial budget is lost when this turn ends.
Your public message this turn is free up to 150 words; beyond that you pay only for the extra length.
You may also replace your last will (free, max 300 words; leave it "" to keep it), e.g. to match a claim you make today. It's shown to everyone if you die.
You may also set your claim (free, max 40 words; leave it "" to keep it): a concise note of what you want everyone to know about you: your claimed role, your night visits and results, and your votes in key trials, e.g. 'Sheriff. N1: checked Bob, Not Evil. N2: checked Dave, Evil. D3: Guilty on Dave'. A new or changed claim appears to everyone as a [Claim] line in the history, and the public ledger lists every player's latest claim and any earlier ones they changed from, as unverified claims.
You are on trial. Everyone else has spoken: this is your last public message before the vote, to answer questions and accusations. This turn is only for discussion: after everyone has spoken, all players vote Guilty/Innocent in a separate, simultaneous vote.

Alice (Ballot Stuffer, claude-opus-5.5) · It is Night 3. Yakuza chat, round 1 of at most 3. Discuss tonight's plan: who holds the Ka · $0.0000
Reasoning (model's thinking) ⓘ
Eight players remain, with Yakuza holding Alice, Frank, and Judy against five non-Yakuza: Carol, Erin, Ivan, Mallory, and Olivia. Bob, revealed as the Jester, gets his revenge tonight — a random Guilty voter from his trial will be struck by a Divine Attack, so I need to work out who voted Guilty.

Judy claimed she voted Innocent, meaning the seven other alive Guilty voters are Alice, Carol, Erin, Frank, Ivan, Mallory, and Olivia — giving Alice or Frank only a 2/7 chance of being hit versus 5/7 for a villager. Combined with tonight's Katana kill, if both strike villagers we'd drop to six players, three Yakuza against three others, which creates a problem: nominations require a majority of six, and Yakuza alone can't reach that threshold, so we'd need at least one villager vote to force a trial, after which my doubled ballot could secure a Guilty majority.

Reassessing claims, I realize Bob being the Jester invalidates his visit counts as fabricated rather than genuine Cartographer data, which actually makes Heidi and Grace's claims (Lookout and Accountant) more credible as real roles, and by extension supports Mallory's Philanthropist claim toward Dave as legitimate. Ivan's vague-then-copying behavior also fits a real Scrutineer pattern, since his stated results (Dave Guilty, Mallory Guilty, Grace Innocent) align plausibly with an early push for a trial.

Thinking through tonight's optimal play: Katana and Ritual kills plus a possible Jester revenge kill could drop villagers from 8 to 5, giving us 3 Yakuza against 2, enough to control nominations and finish them off — though I need to watch for the Jester's revenge hitting the same target as the Katana or even hitting me, though simultaneous resolution should mean my attack still lands and the Katana passes on regardless.

A wrong Ritual guess would publicly expose Judy, and she's already somewhat suspected as "Oracle." Carol's claim as Juror seems plausible given her stated results, though I can't rule out she's faking or is actually some neutral role like an Arsonist or Serial Killer — there's been no failed kill to confirm a Medic exists. For tonight I'm weighing Katana on Ivan, who's suspicious of me as the Scrutineer, against Ritual on Carol as the Juror with a Standard guess, keeping in mind a Medic protecting Carol could cause the Ritual to fail silently without exposing Judy.

I'm also considering alternatives: Katana on Carol with Ritual on Mallory (claimed Philanthropist, gave tokens to Dave) or Ivan (claimed Scrutineer but vaguely). The Jester's revenge pool includes Alice, Carol, Erin, Frank, Ivan, Mallory, and Olivia, so killing two from that list risks a roughly 2/7 chance the revenge boomerangs onto one of our own kills, a 2/7 chance it hits us directly, and a 3/7 chance it strikes another villager — which makes me wonder if a Smuggler-style swap from Frank could redirect that outcome.

Working through the swap math, I realize swapping a pool member with a non-pool player like Judy just shifts where the random revenge lands without any net benefit, and swapping two pool members (like Alice and Carol, or Frank and another villager) is symmetric — whichever one would've been hit just trades places, so there's no actual gain from rearranging who the Katana or revenge targets within the pool.

I'm mapping out D4 scenarios: if katana, ritual, and revenge all hit distinct villagers, we end up 3Y vs 2V and control the outcome entirely, so no token spend needed there. But if revenge instead strikes one of our own kill targets, the math shifts.

With 6 alive and a stuffer vote, nomination still needs 4 Yes and trial needs majority of the 7 votes counted, meaning 4 for majority. We'd have exactly 4 Guilty with the stuffer, but passing a nomination still requires at least one villager going along. If villagers nominate a fellow villager, we pile on; if they try to nominate one of us, they only have 3 votes against our 6, so we simply vote No and the nomination fails.

But if all three of us vote No together, that openly reveals us as a bloc, especially since it's already looking like a 3v3 split. Don't tell() deaths to all. Code tells each player who dies tonight that they were attacked and died, with the kill's cause, at the end of the night; you tell every attacked player who survived, and a player who died about any other Attack on them tonight, failed ones included (R3, R20 step 5). Tell each role-blocked player that they were role-blocked, even one with no night action or who chose not to act (R9); a role-blocker learns only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked (R9). Write private results in the present, about tonight ('You were role-blocked tonight'), never 'last night': they are delivered at the end of this night. Task prompt
It is Day 4, round 1 of at most 8. It's your turn. Your speaking budget is 3.84; you earn 2.5 per round, carrying over up to 8; at the start of each day, 50% of what you have left carries over. You may send one public message and any number of private messages (everyone sees who you messaged, but only the recipient sees the contents), or nothing. The transcript already shows who sent each message, so there's no need to start a message with your own name. Messages are capped at 800 words. Prices grow each round after round 3. The day ends after a full round where nobody sends a public message.
Message prices this round (round 1, 1.00x; next round 1.00x):
   10 words: public 1.17, private 0.29
   25 words: public 1.43, private 0.36
   50 words: public 1.90, private 0.47
  100 words: public 2.92, private 0.73
  200 words: public 5.33, private 1.33
  400 words: public 11.67, private 2.92
  800 words: public 30.33, private 7.58
You may also replace your last will (free, max 300 words; leave it "" to keep it), e.g. to match a claim you make today. It's shown to everyone if you die.
You may also set your claim (free, max 40 words; leave it "" to keep it): a concise note of what you want everyone to know about you: your claimed role, your night visits and results, and your votes in key trials, e.g. 'Sheriff. N1: checked Bob, Not Evil. N2: checked Dave, Evil. D3: Guilty on Dave'. A new or changed claim appears to everyone as a [Claim] line in the history, and the public ledger lists every player's latest claim and any earlier ones they changed from, as unverified claims.
You may nominate a player for trial, which stops chat for a vote. Nominating costs 1.00 from your budget this round and is paid before your messages.

Task prompt
It is Day 4, round 1 of at most 8. It's your turn. Your speaking budget is 0.22; you earn 2.5 per round, carrying over up to 8; at the start of each day, 50% of what you have left carries over. You may send one public message and any number of private messages (everyone sees who you messaged, but only the recipient sees the contents), or nothing. The transcript already shows who sent each message, so there's no need to start a message with your own name. Messages are capped at 800 words. Prices grow each round after round 3. The day ends after a full round where nobody sends a public message.
Message prices during this trial (1.00x):
   10 words: public 1.17, private 0.29
   25 words: public 1.43, private 0.36
   50 words: public 1.90, private 0.47
  100 words: public 2.92, private 0.73
  200 words: public 5.33, private 1.33
  400 words: public 11.67, private 2.92
  800 words: public 30.33, private 7.58
This is a trial turn: prices are 1x whatever the round, and you also get a trial-only budget of 2.00, spent before your regular budget. Unspent trial budget is lost when this turn ends.
Your public message this turn is free up to 150 words; beyond that you pay only for the extra length.
You may also replace your last will (free, max 300 words; leave it "" to keep it), e.g. to match a claim you make today. It's shown to everyone if you die.
You may also set your claim (free, max 40 words; leave it "" to keep it): a concise note of what you want everyone to know about you: your claimed role, your night visits and results, and your votes in key trials, e.g. 'Sheriff. N1: checked Bob, Not Evil. N2: checked Dave, Evil. D3: Guilty on Dave'. A new or changed claim appears to everyone as a [Claim] line in the history, and the public ledger lists every player's latest claim and any earlier ones they changed from, as unverified claims.
You are on trial. Everyone else has spoken: this is your last public message before the vote, to answer questions and accusations. This turn is only for discussion: after everyone has spoken, all players vote Guilty/Innocent in a separate, simultaneous vote.

Tracking changing claims (Frank saying Vanilla in night chat then publicly claiming Scrutineer, Judy revising her guess) was tricky even with the ledger. I also wanted ways to plan with teammates without visible PMs, set conditional night votes, verify Frank's swap before locking my own target, and know how many rounds of night chat to expect, but none of those were available.

I'm noting a few suggestions: display the night chat round count and trial threshold upfront, label targets as "landed on" versus "chose" in the end log, and clarify the revenge/curse rule. I'm also flagging that at 3 Yakuza vs 1 Village the game didn't auto-end despite the outcome being forced, requiring a formality nomination and trial, which seems worth streamlining.

For the unused fields, I'll leave lessons, tips_feedback, and notepad empty, write a short reason, and leave feedback blank. I'm also noting small UI wording quirks like the terse "Night 3: you submitted 1 token(s)" notification and confirming Bob's Jester shows as Evil to the Sheriff, which is expected.

I didn't come close to running out of budget myself, so it wasn't a binding constraint. On Day 3, the nomination happened early in speaking order so I only really spoke during the trial, and since nominations halt discussion immediately, only two public messages went out before trial began—meaning the village gets very limited discussion time, which works in my favor as Yakuza.

I need to pull lessons together from Dave's (Bloodhound) perspective on how the game played out. One key lesson stands out: publicly claiming an exact role with a specific accurate result made me a clear Ritualist target early on, so in the future I should avoid naming other players' exact roles or announcing precise scan results that expose me.

Another lesson involves the Day 2 hang — relying on a single uncorroborated claim and pushing for an execution wasn't urgent when a cheap overnight test was available instead; a count posted early doesn't actually prove innocence, since even Jester or Evil roles could guess correctly on Night 1.

For Bloodhound play, using the token on the disputed claimant was wasteful; better to scent among Vanilla claimants in the N1 holder pool, since a 0 result on a known liar doesn't actually narrow down Jester or non-holder Yakuza. I also shouldn't have announced I'd use a token that night — that gave the wolves the information they needed to kill me first.

On vote-analysis, since all three Yakuza voted honestly with the majority, vote-checking roles like Juror or Scrutineer turned up nothing — so vote consistency checks are unreliable when wolves vote sincerely alongside town.

Trials should target the pool of unverifiable claims — quiet Vanillas and an Oracle whose results are all "wrong" — rather than between competing info-claimants, since that's where the Yakuza hid. And the tip to post exact role/target/result in the first speech actually backfired, since the Ritualist used those public claims to kill Dave and Carol by name.

Keeping tonight's target secret only partially helped since announcing the token spend wasn't necessary for the Ritualist. The Day 2 advice about not naming exact roles was right in principle but the real issue was players self-claiming. The Yakuza tips about voting honestly and not defending a doomed teammate clearly helped them avoid detection by Jurors/Scrutineers since their stated votes matched the totals.

The village claim tip and smuggler's decoy swap both helped. Spending the token on Bob was wasted, and the advice to watch who defends a revealed Yakuza actually hurt since town ended up chasing innocent defenders like Mallory and Olivia, diluting suspicion rather than focusing it—though Alice being among those defenders made it partially useful.

Strategy reviewThe Yakuza (Alice Ballot Stuffer, Frank Smuggler, Judy Ritualist) won without any of them being tried until Day 4, because the Village spent both of its real hangs on a claim fight a Jester started. **Day 2.** Bob (Jester) claimed Cartographer with an invented "one visit" count. When the real Lookout (Heidi) and real Accountant (Grace) contradicted it, he produced a held-back "map" naming Heidi as the Katana holder. The Village accepted "he claimed before any visitor spoke" as proof and wrote off two independent contradicting claims as a double Roleplayer. It refused Heidi's cheap tests (Dave's scent, Mallory's token) and hanged her 9-3. The trial itself came from three vote-info claimants (the real Juror, the real Scrutineer and Frank's fake Scrutineer) asking for "a trial for vote records". **Night 2.** The Yakuza killed the two investigators who could expose them. The Katana took Grace, whose audit would show a teammate's tokens. Judy's ritual took Dave, who had claimed Bloodhound by name and announced a scent. They deliberately left Bob alive as the Day 3 hang. **Day 3.** The Village read the kills as "protecting Bob" and hanged him with 8 Guilty when 5 were needed, even though several players had named the Jester risk. Only Judy stayed Innocent. **Night 3.** The night produced four deaths: - The Katana killed Erin (via Frank's swap). - The ritual killed Carol, who had claimed Juror by name. - The Jester's revenge hit Olivia. - Olivia was the Cardinal, so her curse killed Mallory. **Day 4.** Nine alive had become four: Ivan against three Yakuza. They voted down his nomination of Judy and hanged him. The decisive Village errors were treating an uncorroborated, late, accuser-aimed result as mechanical proof, hanging a likely Jester with every Good player in the revenge pool, and never examining the quiet claims (a Vanilla, an Oracle with only "wrong" guesses, a duplicate Scrutineer). The Yakuza won through discipline: unanimous Katana votes, no day PMs, truthfully stated votes, fake results built only from public information, and both ritual tokens spent on firm exact-role claims.

Outside log review (rules and bugs)
Review: low, rules ambiguityNight 3: the log cannot show whether Bob's Jester revenge was moved by Frank's Olivia/Erin swap. It prints only "[Revenge] Bob's Divine Attack hits Olivia", with no drawn-versus-landed target, and the moderator summary says revenge is "left to code". Both swapped players were in the Guilty-voter pool. R23 says every action aimed at a swapped player moves, but never says whether random post-night effects (Jester/Executioner revenge, Cardinal's curse) count. Frank assumed in Yakuza chat that they do. The "[Night check] Night 3: correct" line also appears before the revenge and the Cardinal's curse resolve, so the check seems not to cover them.
Review: low, harness bugSwap-night labelling is inconsistent. In the Night 3 log the Katana vote reads "attacks Olivia", the resolution line reads "Katana: Alice holds it and attacks Erin", and Alice's result reads "Your Katana attack on Olivia succeeded". Each is defensible under R23, but nothing marks which is the chosen target and which is where it landed. Carol's post-game feedback reports the same problem in the end-of-game action list, which showed her Juror check as Judy + Olivia and the Katana votes as Erin, while her own history showed Judy + Erin and Olivia.
Review: low, rules ambiguityThe Bloodhound text says you learn the three names "and how many Attacks they have made in total this game". That can be read as one number per player or one combined sum. The program gives a single sum ("together they have made 0 attacks"). A non-zero sum would not say which of the three attacked, which changes the role's strength, so the rule should say "combined" explicitly.
Review: low, player confusionNight 2 Yakuza chat: Frank and Judy both treated Bob's fabricated Night 1 Cartographer count as verified. Frank: "Bob's N1 count (one visit) was actually correct, so he's probably a real Cartographer". Judy: "Bob's N1 count was true (one visit), so no Medic acted N1". Yakuza only know their own visits; Night 1 actually had four (Alice->Niaj, Grace->Heidi, Heidi->Ivan, Niaj->Erin). From this they wrongly concluded Grace was a Roleplayer and that no Medic existed, which fed Judy's choice of a 1-token ritual.
Review: low, harness bugDay 3 trial: Bob's updated claim entry was cut off in the public ledger ("D3: Yes on my nomination (earlier \"No\" was a slip), [truncated]"). The claim field has a length limit that silently drops the end of the entry, here his stated trial vote. Players are apparently not warned of the limit, and they use the ledger to track stated votes.
Review: low, otherDay 4: Ivan tried to prove his role by quoting the moderator's private result line verbatim and pointing out that the program lists names alphabetically ("Your scrutiny of Erin, Judy and Olivia: ..."), not target-first as Frank's fake results did. Fixed private-message wording and ordering thus work as an out-of-game way to tell real role-holders from fakes. It changed nothing here because every other voter was Yakuza, but it could decide a closer game on an interface detail.
Game over
WinnersAlice, Frank, Judy, Bob
